title: Add Two Integers
description: Brute force to optimized: simulated step-by-step addition, the built-in operator, then the bitwise XOR and carry trick that mirrors real hardware.

Problem Summary: Given two integers, return their sum, without necessarily using the built-in plus operator.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given two numbers num1 and num2, return their sum, without necessarily using the built-in plus operator.

blocks.title: Analogy: Pushing Two Stacks of Blocks Together
blocks.text: Picture two separate stacks of blocks being pushed together into a single combined stack. The height of the resulting stack is exactly the sum being asked for. This problem is intentionally simple on the surface, its real purpose is usually to explore how that combination can happen, one block at a time, all at once with a built-in operator, or bit by bit the way a circuit inside a computer actually does it.

blocks.caption: Combining two values into their sum

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: num1 = 2, num2 = 3

blocks.text: Example: num1 = 0, num2 = 0
Adding zero to zero gives 0, the simplest possible case.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about why this trivial-looking problem is asked at all.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: This problem's surface difficulty is almost nonexistent, addition is one of the first things any language can do, so the real challenge must be in the constraint of not using the built-in operator.

Observation 2: Addition without carrying is exactly what XOR computes bit by bit, since XOR gives 1 only when the two bits differ, matching how binary digits combine before considering any carry.

Observation 3: A carry is produced exactly where both bits are 1, which is exactly what AND detects, and that carry always needs to be added one bit position further to the left, exactly what a left shift accomplishes.

Observation 4: Repeating XOR and carry-shifting until there is no carry left to add reconstructs the full sum, one layer of carries at a time, which is structurally identical to how a hardware adder circuit is built.
That reasoning alone already reveals the real point of this problem: it is not about computing a sum, it is about explaining how a sum is computed at the bit level.
6. Brute Force Solution

A deliberately naive way to add two numbers without directly using the plus operator on both of them at once is to increase (or decrease) one number by 1, one step at a time, as many times as the other number specifies.
Step by step algorithm

items: If num2 is positive, add 1 to num1, num2 times, one step at a time.
If num2 is negative, subtract 1 from num1 instead, that many times.
Return the running total once every step has been applied.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: simulate addition one single step at a time

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The direction of stepping, incrementing when num2 is positive versus decrementing when it is negative, is chosen specifically so the loop always moves num1 toward the correct final sum regardless of num2's sign.
The loop count is exactly the magnitude of num2, since that magnitude is precisely how many single-unit steps are needed to fully apply it to num1.

This version deliberately avoids using the plus operator directly on the two full numbers, even though it still uses a single-unit increment internally, a controlled relaxation just to make the simulation possible at all.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This works because repeatedly adding or subtracting 1 the correct number of times reconstructs the exact same result as a single addition, just far more slowly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(the size of num2), since it takes one loop iteration per unit of magnitude.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: this is purely a teaching exercise. Every programming language already has a built-in addition operator that performs this exact operation instantly, using dedicated hardware circuitry, there is no reason to simulate it with a loop in practice.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why simulating addition one unit at a time works but is absurd in practice: every language already has a dedicated hardware instruction that performs full addition in a single step, regardless of the numbers' size.

What the loop based version costs: time proportional to the magnitude of one of the numbers, when true addition takes the same constant time no matter how large the numbers are.

Is there ever a real reason not to use the built-in operator: no, for production code the built-in operator is strictly better in every practical way.

So what is left to explore: not a faster way to add, that is already optimal, but a genuine look at how that built-in operator itself works at the bit level.

The core idea: use the built-in operator for real code, but understand the XOR-and-carry mechanism underneath it as separate, purely educational value.

The most practical optimization is simply to use the language's built-in addition operator directly, which is implemented in hardware and runs in constant time regardless of how large the numbers are.
9. Optimized Solution
Return num1 plus num2 directly using the built-in operator.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: the built-in operator does the work in one instant step

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works trivially because the built-in plus operator is defined to compute exactly the mathematical sum of its two operands, using dedicated hardware circuitry that performs the entire addition, including all carry propagation, in a single processor instruction. There is no separate correctness argument needed here, this line of code simply asks the hardware to do what it already does natively.
Code walkthrough

items: There is only one line of logic here specifically because there is nothing left to build once the built-in operator is used directly, any additional code would only be re-implementing what the hardware already provides.
No special casing is needed for negative numbers, zero, or overflow within the representable range, since the built-in operator already handles every one of those cases correctly by definition.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), a single hardware level addition regardless of the size of the numbers.
Space: O(1). For real code, this is the correct answer, and there is nothing left to optimize in practice.
10. Further Optimization: How the Hardware Actually Adds

Since practical optimization already reached O(1), the further value here is purely educational: seeing what the plus operator is doing underneath, using only bitwise operations, which is exactly how addition circuits are built at the hardware level.

Intuition: XOR-ing two bits gives their sum ignoring any carry (0 plus 1 is 1, 1 plus 1 wraps to 0). ANDing two bits tells you exactly where a carry is produced (only when both bits are 1). That carry needs to be added one position further to the left, so the process repeats with the carry as the new second number, until there is no carry left to add.
Dry run for num1 = 2, num2 = 3

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","a","b","Why"],"rows":[["Start","2 (binary 010)","3 (binary 011)","The two starting values before any XOR or carry step has run."],["1","1 (binary 001)","4 (binary 100)","XOR combines the bits that differ, and AND-then-shift produces the new carry to add next."],["2","5 (binary 101)","0 (loop ends)","The carry from the previous step is folded in, and no new carry is produced, so the loop stops."]]}

blocks.text: Once b reaches 0, a holds the final answer, 5, matching the built-in operator exactly.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: XOR for the sum, AND and shift for the carry, repeated until done

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: carry = a & b computes, in a single bitwise operation, every bit position where both numbers currently have a 1, which is exactly and only where a carry gets generated during real binary addition.
a = a ^ b computes the sum of the two numbers at every bit position while deliberately ignoring any carry, exactly what addition without carrying looks like, and precisely what XOR is defined to do.

b = carry shifted left by one moves every detected carry one position over, matching how a carry in ordinary addition always affects the next more significant digit, then the loop feeds that shifted carry back in as the new second number to combine.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of bits), bounded by a small constant for any fixed-width integer type, effectively O(1) in practice.
Space: O(1). This does not beat the built-in operator, its value is purely in understanding what addition looks like at the bit level.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The core lesson here is that even the most basic operation, addition, has a concrete bit level mechanism behind it: combine without carrying using XOR, detect carries using AND, and repeat. This exact XOR-and-carry idea is a common building block in other bit manipulation interview questions.
Common Mistakes

items: Overcomplicating a problem that, in real production code, should simply use the built-in plus operator.
Forgetting that the carry needs to be shifted left by one position before being added back in.

In languages with unbounded integers like Python, forgetting that negative numbers need extra care in a bitwise implementation, since there is no fixed width two's complement representation the way there is in Java or C++.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["One or both numbers being 0","The XOR and carry loop naturally handles this, since XOR-ing with 0 leaves the other number unchanged and no carry is ever produced."],["Negative numbers","Carries and borrows behave differently than with two positive numbers, relying on the fixed-width two's complement representation used in languages like Java and C++."],["Numbers that produce a long chain of carries, like adding 1 to a number made entirely of 1 bits","Exercises the loop's worst case, where the carry keeps propagating one bit further left on every single iteration."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is almost always a setup for the follow up question "now do it without using plus or minus at all". Being ready to walk through the XOR and carry approach confidently, and explaining it as how hardware adders actually work, turns a trivial looking question into a chance to demonstrate real low level understanding.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this without plus or minus", think: XOR for the sum without carry, AND and a left shift for the carry, repeated until there is no carry left.
If the interviewer says "why does this matter if plus already exists", think: this is purely about demonstrating understanding of how a hardware adder circuit actually works.
If the interviewer says "what about negative numbers", think: the bitwise approach relies on a fixed-width two's complement representation, which needs extra care in languages without one, like Python.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Can you explain why XOR alone computes addition without carrying?
Why does the carry always need to be shifted left by exactly one position before being added back in?
How would this bitwise approach need to change in a language without a fixed-width, two's complement integer representation?
Can you trace through what happens when adding two numbers that produce the longest possible chain of carries?
How would you extend this idea to implement subtraction using only bitwise operations?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "implement basic arithmetic without the usual operator" interview question, subtraction, multiplication, or division built from bitwise primitives, which reuses this same XOR-and-carry style of thinking.
Full adder and half adder circuit design in digital logic, the literal hardware equivalent of the XOR-and-carry loop shown here.
Bit manipulation problems in general, where XOR, AND, and shifts combine to express something that looks arithmetic on the surface.
Two's complement representation questions, since the bitwise approach's correctness for negative numbers depends entirely on understanding that representation.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The naive loop based simulation runs in O(the size of num2) time and O(1) space. Both the built-in operator and the bitwise XOR and carry approach run in O(1) time, or O(bits), a small constant, and O(1) space. In real code the built-in operator is always the right choice, the bitwise version exists purely to demonstrate the underlying mechanism.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a trivially simple operation, addition, used as a vehicle to explore its underlying bit-level mechanism.

Core Idea: XOR combines two numbers bit by bit while ignoring any carry, AND detects exactly where a carry is produced, and shifting that carry left and repeating reconstructs the full sum, exactly how a hardware adder circuit works.
Time: O(magnitude of num2) for the brute force, O(1) for the built-in operator, O(number of bits), effectively constant, for the XOR-and-carry version.
Space: O(1) across every version.
Most Important Observation: this problem is rarely about the answer itself, it is almost always a setup for the follow up question asking to avoid plus and minus entirely.
Interview Difficulty: trivial on the surface, but the expected depth is explaining the XOR-and-carry mechanism confidently and clearly.
One line memory trick: XOR adds without carrying, AND finds the carry, shift it left and repeat.
